title: Quantitative Comparison
sub: Quantity A vs. Quantity B — and the secret of answer D

say: Welcome! Today you'll learn a kind of question that school never teaches, but the ISEE loves: quantitative comparison. Two boxes, Quantity A and Quantity B, and you decide which one is bigger.
About fifteen of the thirty-seven questions in the Quantitative Reasoning section look just like this.
Once you learn the trick, these become some of the fastest points on the whole test. Let's go!

steps.html:
Try one first. Just go with your gut!

Quantity A
25% of 80
Quantity B
80% of 25
say: Try one first. Quantity A is twenty-five percent of eighty. Quantity B is eighty percent of twenty-five. Which one is bigger? Just go with your gut.
steps.ok: Hold that thought — we'll check it in a minute.
steps.okSay: Hold that thought. We'll check it in a minute.

steps.html:
The four answers never change:

AQuantity A is greater
BQuantity B is greater
CThey are equal
DCannot be determined
= “It depends!”
say: Here's the first secret. Every comparison question has the same four answers, in the same order. You can memorize them right now.
A means Quantity A is greater.
B means Quantity B is greater.
C means they are equal.
And D means the relationship cannot be determined. That's a fancy way of saying: it depends.

steps.html:
Quantity A
25% of 80
0.25 × 80 = 20
Quantity B
80% of 25
0.8 × 25 = 20

20 = 20 → answer C

Shortcut: x% of y = y% of x. Both are x × y ÷ 100.
say: Now let's check your first answer. Twenty-five percent of eighty is twenty. Eighty percent of twenty-five is also twenty.
Twenty equals twenty, so the answer is C. They are equal.
And here's a shortcut to keep forever: x percent of y always equals y percent of x. Both are just x times y, divided by one hundred.

steps.html:
Your turn. No letters, just numbers:

Quantity A
7 × 8
Quantity B
6 × 9
say: Your turn. Quantity A is seven times eight. Quantity B is six times nine. Which is bigger?
steps.ok: Yes! 7 × 8 = 56 and 6 × 9 = 54. When there are only numbers, it is never D — you can always work it out.
steps.okSay: Yes! Seven times eight is fifty-six, and six times nine is fifty-four. When there are only numbers, the answer is never D. You can always work it out.
steps.no: 7 × 8 = 56 and 6 × 9 = 54, so A is greater. When there are only numbers, it is never D — you can always work it out.
steps.noSay: Not quite. Seven times eight is fifty-six, and six times nine is fifty-four, so A is greater. When there are only numbers, the answer is never D.

steps.html:
So when is it D? When the answer depends.

🐕Dog
vs.
🐈Cat

Which weighs more?

Chihuahua 🐕 < big cat 🐈 → cat
Golden retriever 🐕 > cat 🐈 → dog

Different winners → D
say: So when is the answer D? Only when it truly depends.
Here's a silly example. Which weighs more, a dog or a cat?
Well, a tiny chihuahua weighs less than a big fluffy cat. But a golden retriever weighs a lot more than a cat.
Different examples give different winners. So the answer is: it depends. That's D.

The top line tells you which numbers are allowed.

Your job: plug in allowed numbers and compare.
say: Math questions do the same thing with letters. Here, n is an integer. Quantity A is n squared. Quantity B is n.
The line on top tells you which numbers n is allowed to be. Integers are whole numbers, including zero and negatives.
Your job is to plug in some allowed numbers and see who wins. Let's try it.
Tap a number to plug it in. Try at least two, and watch the winner column.
steps.found: Two different results! n = 3 makes A win, but n = 1 makes them equal. So the answer is D.
steps.foundSay: Look! Some numbers make A win, but others make them equal. Different winners means the answer is D.

steps.html:
The D rule

Find two allowed numbers that give different winners → the answer is D. Stop!

D is not “I don't know” and not “this is hard.”
say: Here's the D rule. If you can find two allowed numbers that give different winners, the answer is D, and you can stop right there.
But be careful. D does not mean I don't know, and it does not mean this is hard. You only pick D when you've actually found two different winners.
Now this one. x can be any number at all. Quantity A is x plus three. Quantity B is x plus one. You don't know x, so is it D? Try at least four numbers and find out.
steps.found: Every number gives the same winner: A. Adding 3 always beats adding 1, whatever x is. So the answer is A, not D!
steps.foundSay: Every number you tried gives the same winner, A. Adding three always beats adding one, no matter what x is. So the answer is A, not D, even though you never knew x.
steps.hint: Try a few more — even weird ones like −10.

steps.html:
Your test kit — numbers where math acts weird:

01½−2100

Only use numbers the top line allows.
say: How do you pick numbers to try? Use your test kit. These are the numbers where math acts weird.
Zero and one, because squaring them doesn't change them.
A fraction like one half, because it shrinks when you square it.
A negative number, like negative two.
And a big number, like one hundred.
Just remember: only use numbers the top line allows.
Here, x is between zero and one. Quantity A is x squared, Quantity B is x. Most kids guess A. Try all three numbers.
steps.found: Surprise! B wins every time. For numbers between 0 and 1, squaring makes them smaller (½ × ½ = ¼). Answer: B.
steps.foundSay: Surprise! B wins every time. For numbers between zero and one, squaring makes them smaller. One half times one half is one quarter. So the answer is B.

steps.html:
Remember

1. The four answers never change: A bigger · B bigger · C equal · D it depends.

2. Only numbers? It's never D — work it out.

3. Letters? Plug in allowed numbers from your test kit: 0, 1, ½, a negative, a big number.

4. Two different winners → D. Same winner every time → that letter.
say: Let's review. The four answers never change: A is bigger, B is bigger, C equal, D it depends.
If there are only numbers, it's never D. Just work it out.
If there are letters, plug in allowed numbers from your test kit: zero, one, one half, a negative, and a big number.
Two different winners means D. The same winner every time means that letter. Awesome work today!
